title: Industry Pulse — AI / Agent Ecosystem

bullets.title: Claude Code 2.1.321 makes Fable 5.2 the default Fable model + adds --settings <file> for remote-control
bullets.summary: Claude Code 2.1.321 (first seen Nov 10) switches the default Fable model to the new Fable 5.2 ($8/$40 per 1M, 1M context, 128k output; optional fast mode up to 2.5x at $16/$80) and adds a --settings <file> flag for `claude remote-control`, alongside a long list of security and reliability fixes; it lands on top of 2.1.319's MCP tasks and denyInsteadOfPrompting.
bullets.how: The Construct: pin per-agent settings files for remote-control/unattended runs, confirm scheduled jobs pick up Fable 5.2 intentionally (cost/latency re-check), keep denyInsteadOfPrompting on. PRAGMA: model-default drift is a client-ops checklist item. Brand 9 Signs: indirect.

bullets.title: Meta ships Muse Ember (Nov 9) — a lightweight 'execution' model for agentic workflows
bullets.summary: Meta positions Muse Ember as a small, fast execution model for the do-the-step side of agent workflows (paired with larger planner models), and it is already listed on OpenRouter and independent benchmark trackers.
bullets.how: The Construct: candidate cheap executor for high-volume Hermes queue sub-steps (planner = Claude, executor = small model) — benchmark on our own tasks before routing anything. PRAGMA: planner/executor split is a client cost-reduction pattern. Brand 9 Signs: no.

bullets.title: Firmly raises $15M Series A (Squarepoint-led; JPMorgan, Mastercard) for agentic commerce + launches Ask Agent
bullets.summary: Seattle's Firmly sells a no-code layer that lets merchants sell and check out inside AI shopping assistants while keeping merchant control over checkout, and launched an 'Ask Agent' product with the round.
bullets.how: Brand 9 Signs: direct fit for the brand9signs.com/shop ChatGPT-shopping work — track Firmly as a possible channel for agent checkout of shop products. PRAGMA: agentic commerce is a live client category. The Construct: watch for an MCP/API.

bullets.title: arXiv 2611.06764: 'Rethinking Access Control for AI Agents: Recent Advances and Open Challenges'
bullets.summary: Survey (Zhou & Zhang, Nov 4) of agent access control across policy specification, identity/delegation, action and resource enforcement, and information-flow control, arguing that the plan an agent picks shapes the permissions it needs, so authorization must be re-assessed as a workflow changes rather than granted once up front.
bullets.how: The Construct: move from static per-agent allowlists toward per-task permission scopes (settings files per job, deny-instead-of-prompt). PRAGMA: frames an 'agent permissions audit' consulting offer. Brand 9 Signs: no.

praxis_lesson: Agent permissions should follow the task, not the agent: give each unattended job its own settings file and deny-by-default scope, and re-check that scope whenever the model or plan underneath it changes.
